network.overall_strategy: Construct ten graph-distinct pathways using experimentally supported Strecker, cyanohydrin, hydantoin and reductive-amination chemistry. Some pathways are experimentally distinct temperature, catalyst or mineral variants of a shared mechanism; they are not ten independent reaction families. The network is complete at a declared feedstock boundary: formaldehyde, HCN, ammonia, glyoxylate, hydroxylamine, hydrogen and reactive mineral inventories are supplied inputs. Their geological production and concentration are not assumed solved, especially for glyoxylate, HCN and hydroxylamine. Competing glycolate formation and secondary glycine consumption are explicit. All settings are anoxic; surface reactions not requiring irradiation occupy water-covered or mineral-shaded locations. Neutral organic acids and NH3 represent analytical acid-base pools rather than their dominant microspecies. Fe(OH)2 and FeOOH represent idealized ferrous and ferric mineral endmember equivalents; they conserve atoms and reducing equivalents without asserting that every experiment produces a pure FeOOH phase. Initial ferric material is an explicitly declared boundary inventory, not material generated using molecular oxygen within this network. A single representative environment_formed is assigned where several environments are possible; null denotes an unspecified boundary origin. Glycine denotes chemical identity, including mineral-associated material, not necessarily freely available dissolved product. The role intermediate also covers terminal coproducts because the schema has no byproduct category. Conditions distinguish reported experimental anchors from proposed screening windows. Slow hydrolysis, mineral passivation, feedstock supply and product desorption remain explicit bottlenecks.

reactions.name: Reversible formaldehyde-ammonia condensation

conditions.other: Design window: pH 8-9; formaldehyde 1-100 mM and total ammonia 50-500 mM; hours to days with immediate downstream cyanide trapping. Use a covered or water-shaded pool with limited gas exchange. These concentrations and residence times are screening assumptions, not measured geological inventories.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to formaldehyde; the resulting carbinolamine reversibly loses water to form methanimine.
reactions.reasoning: This is the conventional condensation component of Strecker chemistry underlying reducing-atmosphere amino-acid experiments (Miller, 1953; Johnson et al., 2008). Methanimine need not accumulate or be isolated: hydration and hydrolysis compete strongly in water. Concentrated, retained ammonia and formaldehyde remain feedstock assumptions, not consequences of those experiments.

reactions.name: Cyanide trapping of methanimine

conditions.other: Design window: pH 8-9; total cyanide 10-100 mM; total ammonia comparable to or greater than total cyanide. Couple directly to rxn_001 without isolating methanimine; hours-to-days screening residence. HCN volatilization and hydroxy-nitrile formation must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the imine or iminium carbon, with proton transfer yielding aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile formation is the chemically established core of the aqueous Strecker interpretation of Miller-type experiments (Miller, 1953; Johnson et al., 2008). No mineral catalyst is required. The amino-acid branch is not intrinsically exclusive: formaldehyde also enters rxn_003, and feedstock concentrations cannot be inferred from amino-acid detection alone.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Design window: pH 7-9; formaldehyde and total cyanide each 10-100 mM; hours-to-days screening residence. Formation is reversible. Low ammonia favors storage as cyanohydrin rather than immediate aminonitrile formation.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the formaldehyde carbonyl, followed by proton transfer to form glycolonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Glycolonitrile is an experimentally grounded branch point in cyanide-derived precursor chemistry (Patel et al., 2015). This reaction requires neither UV photoredox catalysis nor sulfide because the formaldehyde is already supplied. It creates both a productive ammonia-exchange route and the competing glycolate route, rather than a guaranteed glycine precursor.

reactions.name: Ammonia-driven conversion of glycolonitrile to aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Design window: pH 8-9; glycolonitrile 10-100 mM; total ammonia 0.1-0.5 M; hours to days. Introduce ammonia before strong heating or acid hydrolysis. Required ammonia retention and transfer between precursor-rich and ammonia-rich waters are scenario assumptions.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanohydrin-carbonyl equilibration, ammonia condensation and renewed cyanide trapping give net replacement of hydroxyl by amino functionality; direct displacement of free hydroxide is not assumed.
reactions.reasoning: Ammonia conversion of glycolonitrile into the aminonitrile branch is supported by the cyanosulfidic precursor network (Patel et al., 2015). This node represents only the downstream exchange chemistry, not the upstream Cu/sulfide/UV homologation sequence. Cu is therefore not assigned as an unjustified catalyst, and this pathway is acknowledged to share Strecker equilibria with P1.

reactions.name: Aminoacetonitrile hydration to glycinamide
agents: Hydronium supplied by an anoxic volcanic acid pool

conditions.other: Proposed hydrolysis window: pH 0-2 and 1-30 days. Transfer or acidify an aminonitrile-bearing fraction after precursor formation; do not assume coexistence with the alkaline synthesis stage. The supplied research does not establish a rate constant within this entire window.

reactions.mechanism: Protonation and water addition to the nitrile, followed by tautomerization, produce glycinamide.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile-to-amide-to-amino-acid hydrolysis is the standard Strecker product-release sequence (Miller, 1953; Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013). The acid pool is an accelerator, not a required mineral catalyst. Environmental execution remains conditional because acid availability, transfer losses and hydrolysis kinetics must be established; rapid neutral-water hydrolysis is not assumed.

reactions.name: Glycinamide hydrolysis to glycine
agents: Hydronium supplied by an anoxic volcanic acid pool

conditions.other: Proposed window: pH 0-2 and 1-30 days, with analytical monitoring rather than an assumed complete conversion. Ammonia is predominantly ammonium here. Cool and neutralize only if subsequent chemistry requires it; those operations are not additional synthesis reactions.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the activated amide carbonyl; carbon-nitrogen bond cleavage releases glycine and the ammonia/ammonium pool.
reactions.reasoning: This is the terminal hydrolysis of the established aminonitrile route (Miller, 1953; Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013). Amide hydrolysis can be the product-release bottleneck and must not be treated as instantaneous at ambient neutral pH. Nitrogen originally residing in the nitrile is released, whereas the amino nitrogen is retained in glycine.

reactions.name: Carbon dioxide trapping of aminoacetonitrile as hydantoin

conditions.other: Provisional substrate-specific window: pH 8-9; dissolved inorganic carbon 10-100 mM; aminonitrile 1-100 mM; ammonia-rich solution; hours to days. Carbon dioxide denotes the inorganic-carbon pool. Retention of both inorganic carbon and cyanide-derived intermediates must be verified.

reactions.mechanism: Aminonitrile carbamylation, cyclization through an imino heterocycle and rearrangement incorporate inorganic carbon into hydantoin.
reactions.reasoning: Bucherer-Bergs chemistry supports aminonitrile-to-hydantoin conversion, and related prebiotic experiments support hydantoin-mediated amino-acid production (Pulletikurti et al., 2022; Ferris et al., 1974). However, the 2022 study emphasizes alpha-ketoacid substrates. Applying its mild formation conditions specifically to unsubstituted hydantoin from formaldehyde-derived aminoacetonitrile is a provisional extrapolation, not a demonstrated yield claim.

reactions.name: Hydantoin ring opening to N-carbamoylglycine
agents: Hydronium in a separate acidic geothermal pool

conditions.other: Proposed window: pH 0-2; 1-30 days, extending only if measured survival and conversion justify it. Requires acidification or transfer from the carbonate-rich formation stage. Ring-opening kinetics for unsubstituted hydantoin under these exact conditions are unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic cleavage of the cyclic amide opens hydantoin to N-carbamoylglycine.
reactions.reasoning: Hydantoin hydrolysis provides a recognized connection to amino acids (Ferris et al., 1974; Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013). The approximately 353 K hydrolysis discussed for other hydantoin systems cannot automatically establish the rate for this substrate (Pulletikurti et al., 2022). This is therefore an explicit kinetic bottleneck with provisional environmental operating conditions.

reactions.name: N-carbamoylglycine hydrolysis and carbon dioxide release
agents: Hydronium in a separate acidic geothermal pool

conditions.other: Proposed window: pH 0-2 and 1-30 days. Monitor residual ureido compound, glycine and total ammonia. Carbon dioxide loss can favor net deprotection, but conversion and product survival cannot be assigned without substrate-specific kinetic measurements.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the carbamoyl group releases glycine; the remaining carbamic-acid equivalent decomposes to ammonia and carbon dioxide.
reactions.reasoning: This represents the conventional terminal chemistry of hydantoin hydrolysis to glycine (Ferris et al., 1974; Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013). The split into ring opening and decarbamoylation makes the slow steps visible, rather than interpreting hydantoin formation as immediate amino-acid production. Exact prebiotic rates remain unsupported by the supplied substrate-specific evidence.

reactions.name: Moderate-temperature hydrothermal Strecker synthesis, lumped
agents: Pyrite-pyrrhotite-magnetite assemblage as a redox buffer, not a demonstrated reaction catalyst

conditions.other: Reported anchors: NH4Cl-containing solution, CO2/H2 gas mixture of 3:1, and 25-54 h residence. Initial reactant concentrations and pH are not securely specified in the supplied summary. Require a locally sulfide-bearing subseafloor pocket and subsequent cooling; do not extrapolate to prolonged residence above 473 K.

reactions.mechanism: Lumped imine formation, cyanide addition and nitrile/amide hydrolysis. Ammonia appears on both sides because amino nitrogen is incorporated while nitrile nitrogen is released.
reactions.reasoning: Hennet et al. (1992) reported hydrothermal Strecker synthesis; the supplied 9.3-11.6 mM glycine values are available through Andersson and Holm (2000), not direct verification of the primary paper. This is a temperature-regime variant of Strecker chemistry, not a new mechanism. Thermal destruction limits extrapolation to hotter vents (Bada et al., 1995; Aubrey et al., 2009).

reactions.name: Reversible glyoxylate-ammonia condensation to glycine imine

conditions.temperature: 293-343 K, selected to match the coupled reduction
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm, or 5 bar H2 when coupled to hydrogenation
conditions.other: pH 8-10; total ammonia 6-375 mM depending on the downstream experiment. Condensation occurs in situ during reduction, not as an isolated preparative stage. Residence follows the coupled reaction, from laboratory day-scale screening to six-week mineral incubations.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to glyoxylate through a hemiaminal; reversible dehydration generates a low-abundance imine pool.
reactions.reasoning: Glycine imine has been characterized, and its rapid hydration or hydrolysis in water is documented (Paczelt et al., 2023). Coupled reductive amination does not require an isolable bulk imine concentration (Kaur et al., 2024). The node is a mechanistic bookkeeping intermediate that may be surface-bound; efficient geological glyoxylate supply remains unresolved.

reactions.name: Hydrogenation of glycine imine over supported nickel
agents: Reduced Ni(0) on SiO2-Al2O3, approximately 10 mol% Ni relative to starting carbonyl substrate

conditions.other: Reported anchors: pH 8 and total ammonium 6-150 mM. Couple to rxn_011 in an anoxic, hydrogen-retaining mineral-interface reactor. A 24-72 h screening residence is proposed, not asserted as a glyoxylate-specific time course from the supplied report. Measure nickel passivation and rxn_020 concurrently.

reactions.mechanism: Nickel dissociates hydrogen and transfers surface hydrogen to the imine carbon-nitrogen bond.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrogen-driven amino-acid production over supported nickel is experimentally supported at low ammonium concentrations (Kaur et al., 2024). Reported amino-plus-hydroxy-acid yields are not glycine-only yields, and glycolate competes. The supported catalyst is a laboratory benchmark; equivalent activity on an unmodified natural nickel-bearing mineral is an unproven geological extrapolation.

reactions.name: Hydrogenation of glycine imine on meteoritic Fe-Ni material
agents: Ground iron meteorite containing accessible metallic Fe-Ni surfaces

conditions.other: Reported framework: pH 8 and ammonium in the 6-150 mM experimental range. Use an anoxic hydrogen-retaining pore or experimental analog. A 1-7 day screening interval is proposed. Meteorite identity, exposed Ni(0), surface area and loading require specification; the supplied summary does not provide a transferable loading-rate relationship.

reactions.mechanism: Accessible meteoritic metal sites activate hydrogen and reduce the coupled glyoxylate-derived imine.
reactions.reasoning: Ground iron meteorites were tested as catalysts in hydrogen-driven reductive amination (Kaur et al., 2024), giving this variant a more direct material analog than synthetic supported nickel. Meteorites are not interchangeable catalysts: corrosion, passivation and accessible nickel determine performance. This is a catalyst-distinct pathway sharing the hydrogenation mechanism of P5.

reactions.name: Glycine imine reduction by mixed-valence iron hydroxides
agents: Initially mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) hydroxide precipitate; ferrous sites are consumed as reducing equivalents

conditions.catalyst: Mixed-valence hydroxide interface; not a regenerated ferrous reductant
conditions.other: Reported anchors: glyoxylate 2.5 mM, NH4Cl 375 mM, pH 7-10, and approximately 50% initial Fe(II) for substantial glycine/glycolate production. Use week-scale monitoring. Initial Fe(III) is a declared boundary inventory; an anoxic source such as prior photochemical Fe(II) oxidation is a geological assumption, not demonstrated here.

reactions.mechanism: Ferrous mineral sites provide the reducing equivalents for imine hydrogenation and become ferric sites; the initial ferric component also supplies the mixed-valence interface.
reactions.reasoning: The glyoxylate experiments are reported by Barge et al. (2020), whereas Barge et al. (2019) primarily addressed pyruvate. Near-equal glycine and glycolate production makes rxn_021 essential. FeOOH on both sides preserves the explicitly required initial ferric inventory while recording additional oxidation; the endmember balance does not establish the final mineral assemblage.

reactions.name: Glycine imine reduction by ferroan brucite
agents: Ferroan brucite, nominal Fe0.33Mg0.67(OH)2; structural Fe(II) is the finite reductant and the Mg-bearing host is not consumed in the represented redox balance

conditions.catalyst: Ferroan brucite reactive interface; structural Fe(II) is consumed
conditions.other: Reported anchors: starting pH 10, glyoxylate 100 mM, NH4Cl 100 mM, and six weeks. The reported ferrous inventory could support at most 31.25 mM amino acid. Couple directly to rxn_011. Quantify dissolved and mineral-associated glycine separately, together with glycolate and secondary amination products.

reactions.mechanism: Structural Fe(II) transfers reducing equivalents to the imine; oxidation of the mineral supplies the net hydrogen equivalents needed to form glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Ferroan brucite supports glycine synthesis with ammonia under mild conditions (Chimiak et al., 2024). The reported 52-69% yields must be interpreted using the study's limiting-reagent basis, not as 52-69 mM glycine from 100 mM glyoxylate when Fe(II) permits only 31.25 mM. Mineral availability, long residence and independent replication remain limitations.

reactions.name: Coupled nitrate reduction and glyoxylate amination on ferroan brucite
agents: Ferroan brucite, nominal Fe0.33Mg0.67(OH)2, as a stoichiometrically consumed electron source and reactive interface

conditions.catalyst: Ferroan brucite interface; Fe(II) is not regenerated
conditions.other: Reported anchors: glyoxylate 100 mM, KNO3 100 mM, starting pH 10, and six weeks. The reported Fe(II) inventory supports at most 6.25 mM glycine for this nitrogen source. The proton input is formal charge bookkeeping at controlled pH, not an acidic bulk solution. Distinguish acid-digestible total product from dissolved product.

reactions.mechanism: A lumped coupled process reduces nitrate-derived nitrogen and incorporates it into reduced glyoxylate. Nitrogen reduction and carbonyl reduction together require substantially more electrons than ammonia-based amination.
reactions.reasoning: This coupled route was demonstrated with ferroan brucite (Chimiak et al., 2024). The graph does not assert that free ammonia accumulates as an isolated intermediate. Reported glycine yields were low, and up to 97% of product in nitrate systems was mineral-associated and recovered after acid digestion; synthesis therefore does not establish downstream bioavailability.

reactions.name: Glyoxylate condensation with hydroxylamine

conditions.other: Proposed screening window: pH 4-7, glyoxylate 10-100 mM, hydroxylamine at least comparable to glyoxylate, and hours to days. These are design conditions rather than a verified reproduction of the primary experimental recipe. Couple to native-iron reduction without requiring oxime isolation.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine adds to the aldehyde group and loses water to form a glyoxylic acid oxime.
reactions.reasoning: Hydroxylamine plus metallic iron was used to obtain amino acids from ketoacids, including glyoxylate (Muchowska et al., 2019). Oxime formation is the conventional mechanistic interpretation, but the supplied research does not establish an isolated oxime time course under these conditions. Geological hydroxylamine supply and persistence are additional boundary assumptions.

reactions.name: Native-iron reduction of glyoxylic acid oxime
agents: Native Fe(0) powder or exposed meteoritic iron, acting as a consumed reductant and reactive surface

conditions.catalyst: Reactive Fe(0) surface; iron is consumed rather than assumed catalytic
conditions.other: Proposed window: pH 4-7 and hours-to-days monitoring. Supply enough accessible Fe(0) for oxime reduction, plus independently assessed corrosion losses. Buffered proton activity, not an unbuffered proton stock, supports the formal ionic balance. Surface passivation and dissolved Fe(II) must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Reduction cleaves the nitrogen-oxygen bond and saturates the carbon-nitrogen bond; Fe(0) is oxidized to Fe(II), with oxygen leaving as water.
reactions.reasoning: The overall hydroxylamine/metallic-iron amino-acid synthesis is supported by Muchowska et al. (2019). This node exposes reductant consumption that would be hidden by labeling iron only as a catalyst. The isolated-oxime mechanism and stated screening pH/time window are provisional decompositions of the experimentally supported overall transformation.

reactions.name: Competing glycolonitrile hydrolysis to glycolate

conditions.other: Same proposed pH 0-2 and 1-30 day hydrolysis window as the aminonitrile branch. This sink acts on glycolonitrile that escapes ammonia conversion. The amino/hydroxy product split is established partly during precursor formation, not only during hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis release glycolic acid and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanohydrin chemistry competes with aminoacetonitrile formation in cyanide-derived networks (Patel et al., 2015; Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013). Explicit glycolate production prevents the model from treating every cyanide-formaldehyde encounter as productive glycine synthesis. Exact rates must be determined in the same matrix used for rxn_005 and rxn_006.

reactions.name: Competing hydrogenation of glyoxylate to glycolate
agents: Ni(0)/SiO2-Al2O3 or characterized meteoritic Fe-Ni metal, used as alternative catalysts rather than a required mixture

conditions.catalyst: The same metal catalyst used in the coupled reductive-amination experiment
conditions.other: pH 8; total ammonium 6-150 mM; match catalyst loading, surface state and residence to rxn_012 or rxn_013. Measure amino-acid and hydroxy-acid production independently. Reduced ammonia availability increases the importance of direct carbonyl reduction.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-activated hydrogen reduces the glyoxylate carbonyl directly, bypassing nitrogen incorporation.
reactions.reasoning: Amino-acid and hydroxy-acid production compete in the nickel and meteorite experiments (Kaur et al., 2024). Combined product yields cannot be assigned entirely to glycine. This sink shares the same hydrogen inventory and active surface as productive imine hydrogenation, so selectivity must be modeled jointly.

reactions.name: Competing mineral-driven glyoxylate reduction to glycolate
agents: Fe(II)-bearing hydroxide interface: either mixed-valence iron hydroxides or ferroan brucite in separate experiments

conditions.temperature: 343 K for the mixed-hydroxide system; 293 K for ferroan brucite
conditions.catalyst: Reactive iron hydroxide interface; ferrous reducing equivalents are consumed
conditions.other: Match pH, ammonium, mineral loading and duration to rxn_014 or rxn_015. These are two experimental settings, not a validated continuous temperature-response curve. Quantify glycolate against glycine and include competition for the finite Fe(II) inventory.

reactions.mechanism: Electron and proton transfer from ferrous mineral sites reduces the carbonyl group directly while oxidizing Fe(II) to Fe(III).
reactions.reasoning: Glycolate is a documented competitor in iron-hydroxide and ferroan-brucite glyoxylate experiments (Barge et al., 2020; Chimiak et al., 2024). In the mixed-valence system it can be comparable to glycine. Including its reductant demand prevents overestimating the amino-acid yield permitted by the mineral electron budget.

reactions.name: Secondary reductive amination consuming glycine
agents: Ferroan brucite with remaining accessible structural Fe(II)

conditions.catalyst: Ferroan brucite reactive interface; structural Fe(II) is consumed
conditions.other: Starting pH approximately 10; glyoxylate-rich mixtures; days to six weeks, matching the brucite incubations. Requires both residual glyoxylate and remaining mineral reducing capacity after glycine first forms. Product formation is not assumed if glycine is inaccessible through adsorption.

reactions.mechanism: Glycine's amino group condenses with another glyoxylate molecule; reduction of the resulting imine yields iminodiacetic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Iminodiacetic acid was identified among ferroan-brucite reaction products (Chimiak et al., 2024). Secondary reductive amination is a chemically justified interpretation, although the isolated sequence was not established by the supplied evidence. This explicitly represents loss of accumulated glycine and additional consumption of the finite ferrous inventory.

pathways.name: Aqueous imine-first Strecker pathway
pathways.description: Form methanimine in an ammonia-rich pool, trap it with cyanide, and hydrolyze the aminonitrile through glycinamide. The alkaline precursor stage and acidic heated hydrolysis stage require sequential conditions or physical transfer; they are not simultaneous one-pot conditions.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-first ammonia-exchange pathway
pathways.description: Store formaldehyde and cyanide as glycolonitrile, introduce ammonia before hydrolysis, and converge on aminoacetonitrile. This is a distinct precursor-processing path sharing Strecker equilibria with P1, not an independent elementary mechanism. Residual glycolonitrile is lost through rxn_019.

pathways.name: Hydantoin capture and hydrolytic release pathway
pathways.description: Capture formaldehyde-derived aminoacetonitrile with inorganic carbon, then open and hydrolyze hydantoin to glycine. The formaldehyde-specific mild formation window and environmental hydrolysis rates are provisional; evidence for other hydantoin substrates is not treated as a measured rate for this sequence.

pathways.name: Moderate-temperature hydrothermal Strecker pathway
pathways.description: Use the experimentally reported 423 K hydrothermal setting for coupled precursor reaction and hydrolysis, represented as one lumped reaction. This temperature-regime variant requires cooling for accumulation and is not extrapolated to black-smoker temperatures.

pathways.name: Hydrogen-supported nickel reductive amination
pathways.description: Couple in situ glyoxylate-ammonia condensation to hydrogenation on supported Ni(0). This is an experimentally supported low-ammonium laboratory benchmark with an unresolved natural-catalyst analog. Direct glycolate formation through rxn_020 shares the same reductant.

pathways.name: Hydrogen-supported meteoritic metal reductive amination
pathways.description: Couple the same imine-forming equilibrium to hydrogenation on characterized meteoritic Fe-Ni surfaces. This is a catalyst-distinct experimental variant of P5, contingent on accessible metal sites, sustained hydrogen pressure and limited passivation.

pathways.name: Mixed-valence iron-hydroxide reductive amination
pathways.description: Reduce the glyoxylate-derived imine using ferrous sites in an initially mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) interface. Initial ferric inventory is supplied explicitly rather than generated by an undeclared oxygen exposure. Glycolate competes for the same ferrous inventory through rxn_021.

pathways.name: Ammonia-fed ferroan-brucite reductive amination
pathways.description: Form and reduce the imine within an ammonia-containing ferroan-brucite suspension at approximately 293 K. Structural Fe(II), not glyoxylate alone, limits yield. Long residence, competing glycolate production and secondary glycine consumption must be included in any accumulation model.

pathways.name: Nitrate-fed ferroan-brucite coupled nitrogen reduction
pathways.description: Use nitrate rather than supplied ammonia in a coupled mineral-mediated reduction and amination. The greater electron demand lowers the maximum glycine yield for a fixed Fe(II) inventory. The target includes mineral-associated glycine; acid-digestion recovery is not evidence that free glycine was environmentally available.

pathways.name: Hydroxylamine-oxime pathway with native iron
pathways.description: Condense glyoxylate with hydroxylamine and reduce the resulting oxime using consumable Fe(0). The overall reagent combination is experimentally supported, while the isolated intermediate sequence and proposed operating window require verification. Hydroxylamine supply is an additional unresolved feedstock boundary.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a coherent, well-established Strecker route supported by the supplied classical aqueous Strecker literature. Methanimine is appropriately represented as a reversible, transient intermediate rather than an abundant isolated reagent. The principal unresolved issue is whether aminoacetonitrile and glycinamide hydrolysis proceed sufficiently rapidly in the intended surface setting: reaction-specific pH, temperature and residence times are not supplied.
suggestions: Specify pH, temperature, reagent concentrations and residence times for formation and hydrolysis, distinguishing measured conditions from proposed operating windows.
Quantify nitrile and amide conversion alongside competing formaldehyde chemistry and glycolate production before predicting glycine accumulation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanohydrin formation followed by ammonia-dependent aminonitrile formation is consistent with the supplied Strecker and Patel et al. (2015) discussion. rxn_004 is credible as a net conversion through aqueous equilibria, without requiring an elementary displacement of hydroxide. Upstream photoredox chemistry is unnecessary at the declared feedstock boundary. The explicit glycolate branch, rxn_019, correctly captures a selectivity loss, but its competition with productive conversion is unquantified.
suggestions: Parameterize aminonitrile versus cyanohydrin partitioning using ammonia concentration, pH, temperature and reaction time.
Provide hydrolysis conditions and rates for both the productive nitrile branch and competing rxn_019.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The five-step sequence is inferred as imine-first aminonitrile formation followed by rxn_007–rxn_009. Bucherer–Bergs capture and eventual hydantoin hydrolysis are chemically credible. However, Pulletikurti et al. (2022) studied alpha-ketoacid-derived chemistry; its reported operating conditions do not directly establish hydrolysis rates for this unsubstituted hydantoin/N-carbamoylglycine sequence. A Surface label alone does not establish an effective hydrolytic release regime.
suggestions: Attach explicit reaction-ID sequences to pathways and cite substrate-specific evidence for aminoacetonitrile-to-hydantoin conversion.
Establish pH, temperature and residence-time requirements for both hydrolysis steps rather than transferring mild conditions from differently substituted hydantoins.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The lumped reaction is a valid representation of hydrothermal Strecker synthesis, and ammonia appearing on both sides does not invalidate it. The supplied Hennet et al. (1992) evidence supports glycine formation around 150 degrees C and 10 bar, although the quantitative results are reported through Andersson and Holm (2000). Those numerical conditions are not actually attached to rxn_010 in the submitted network.
suggestions: Specify temperature, pressure, gas composition, ammonia concentration and residence time, with a citation distinguishing primary from secondary evidence.
Describe the pyrite–pyrrhotite–magnetite assemblage as an experimental redox buffer rather than a demonstrated essential catalyst, and avoid unsupported extrapolation to hotter systems.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024, Chem) strongly supports the overall hydrogen-driven reductive amination chemistry. Glycine imine should remain an equilibrating mechanistic intermediate, consistent with Paczelt et al. (2023), rather than an assumed stable stock. Environmental confidence is lower because the supported nickel material and hydrogen confinement are not defined for the stated environment. Competing rxn_020 also requires an active hydrogenation catalyst; molecular hydrogen alone is insufficient under the cited mild conditions.
suggestions: Attach the experimental anchor of approximately 22 degrees C, pH 8 and 5 bar hydrogen, with catalyst support, loading and reaction time.

Identify a physically available active nickel material and explicitly assign its catalytic role to both rxn_012 and rxn_020; keep synthetic supported nickel distinct from an untested natural analogue.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The meteorite-mediated variant is supported by the supplied Kaur et al. (2024) evidence and is legitimately distinct as an experimental catalyst variant, not a new reaction family. Its implementation remains conditional on accessible active metal surfaces, adequate hydrogen availability and limited passivation. The shared glycolate reaction is chemically appropriate when assigned to the same active metal catalyst.
suggestions: Specify meteorite composition, particle size, exposed metal fraction and the relevant experimental catalyst preparation.
Define hydrogen pressure or dissolved concentration, confinement and passivation timescales, and measure amino-acid versus hydroxy-acid selectivity.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Barge et al. (2020, JGR Planets) directly supports glyoxylate-to-glycine chemistry on mixed-valence iron hydroxides. The declared endmember representation and initial ferric boundary inventory are acceptable abstractions and do not require oxygen generation within the network. Fe(II) supplies reducing equivalents rather than acting as an indefinitely reusable catalyst. The actual mineral composition, ferric fraction and operating conditions remain unspecified.
suggestions: Specify mineral preparation, Fe(II)/Fe(III) ratio, ammonia concentration, pH and temperature using the glycine-specific 2020 study.
Separate the initial ferric inventory from newly oxidized iron and model finite Fe(II) capacity, passivation and competition through rxn_021.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chimiak et al. (2024) provides direct experimental support for ammonia-fed ferroan-brucite glycine synthesis. Representing reactive mineral Fe(II) by Fe(OH)2 equivalents is acceptable under the stated abstraction; omitted spectator magnesium is not itself a conservation objection. Glycolate and iminodiacetate are well-motivated competing products. Quantitative performance remains conditional on mineral capacity and multiweek kinetics, and the supplied evidence is from a recent single-laboratory study.
suggestions: Attach the reported approximate 20 degrees C, initial pH 10 and multiweek reaction duration, clearly separating these from proposed screening conditions.
Specify reactive Fe(II) inventory and mineral composition, report yield denominators explicitly, and quantify product loss through rxn_022.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The coupled nitrate route has direct support in Chimiak et al. (2024). Ten Fe(II) equivalents are chemically reasonable: eight electrons reduce nitrate nitrogen to the amine oxidation state and two reduce the carbonyl/imine functionality. rxn_016 should be interpreted as an empirical net reaction, not an elementary mechanism. Low reported yields limit flux confidence, while mineral association does not defeat the explicitly defined chemical-identity target. Formal proton accounting does not itself imply an acidic environment.
suggestions: Specify nitrate and glyoxylate concentrations, mineral loading, pH evolution and reaction duration, with electron-limited maximum yields.
Distinguish dissolved glycine from mineral-associated, acid-extractable glycine without equating analytical digestion with environmental desorption.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Oxime formation followed by native-iron reduction is chemically plausible and consistent with the hydroxylamine/iron experiments of Muchowska et al. (2019). The supplied summary supports the overall transformation more directly than it establishes every discrete intermediate. The balance audit accepts rxn_018; its remaining issues concern operating conditions, iron corrosion/passivation and the separately flagged mol_020 identity metadata. Hydroxylamine supply is an acknowledged boundary assumption, not an omitted mandatory synthesis step.
suggestions: Normalize mol_020 to one iron atom with charge +2, for example using the structural representation [Fe+2], and reconcile its formula and InChI.
Specify pH, temperature, iron surface preparation and reagent concentrations, and distinguish direct oxime evidence from mechanistic inference.

evaluation.network_feedback: This is a credible, connected glycine-synthesis network at its declared feedstock boundary, but it is not approved at the 0.90 network threshold. All 25 molecule nodes participate, IDs are used consistently in the reaction list, and complete productive routes reach mol_015. Accepting the deterministic audit as instructed, all 22 reaction sets are balanced or balanceable and none is classified as a conservation violation. The mol_020 formula/structure discrepancy requires metadata repair, not rejection of rxn_018. Neutral acid-base pools, mineral endmember equivalents and the initial ferric boundary inventory are reasonable declared abstractions. The supplied literature supports the principal chemistry, and the network appropriately acknowledges upstream supply limitations, competing glycolate production, glycine consumption, passivation and mineral binding. No penalty is assigned for the selected feedstocks, shared mechanisms, pathway count or environment count.
